```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
pkgload::load_all()

# Prevent noto serif from being chosen
systemfonts::register_variant(name = "sans", family = "Liberation Sans")
bayesplot::bayesplot_theme_set(bayesplot::theme_default(base_size = 11, base_family = "sans"))
set.seed(42)

# Reproucible plotting across systems
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev = "ragg_png",
  fig.path = "man/figures/README-",
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.width = 7.5,
  fig.height = 3.75,
  dpi = 125
)

# Determine active git branch for dynamic badges
branch = Sys.getenv("GITHUB_REF_NAME", "")

}

# Link README figures to the pkgdown site (which renders them) instead of committing them
knitr::knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options) knitr::hook_plot_md(sub("^man/", paste0(site_url, "reference/"), x), options))
```

# mcp: Regression with Multiple Change Points<img src="man/figures/logo_200px.png" align="right" style="padding: 20px; padding-right: 0px;"/>

`r sprintf("[![mcp Github Actions status](https://github.com/lindeloev/mcp/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml/badge.svg?branch=%s)](https://github.com/lindeloev/mcp/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml?query=branch%%3A%s)", branch, branch)` `r sprintf("[![mcp Codecov status](https://codecov.io/gh/lindeloev/mcp/branch/%s/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/lindeloev/mcp/branch/%s)", branch, branch)` [![mcp CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/mcp)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mcp) [![mcp CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/mcp)](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/mcp)

`mcp` is regression with multiple change points, inferring full Bayesian uncertainty for all parameters, including the change points themselves. At its simplest, it feels like `lm()` with one formula per segment. At its most flexible, it aims to be [**`brms`**](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) **for change points**:

- *GLMM and distributional regression:* Gaussian, binomial, Bernoulli, Poisson, and Negative Binomial families. Group-level (random) effects, AR/MA, and regression on distributional parameters (e.g., `sigma`, `shape`).

- *Express expert knowledge:* Specify the number of change points, the form of each segment, and restrict coefficients via priors. Compare hypotheses using `loo()` and `hypothesis()`.

- *Native feel:* `summary()`, `plot_pars()`, `pp_check()`, and `as_draws_df()` follow the conventions of [`brms`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/), [`rstanarm`](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/), and [`posterior`](https://mc-stan.org/posterior/articles/posterior.html), adapted to change point regression. Inspect the sampled JAGS model in `fit$jags_code`.

`mcp` has [200+ academic citations](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cites=5590697509718421309) across ecology, astronomy, neuroscience, epidemiology, and other disciplines. You will find many aliases for change point regression in the literature, including piecewise linear, discontinuity, segmented, and broken stick regression.

# Install

Install `mcp` from CRAN:

``` r
install.packages("mcp")
```

or install the development version from GitHub:

``` r
if (!requireNamespace("remotes")) install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lindeloev/mcp@dev")
```

`mcp` uses JAGS through `rjags`. If installation of `rjags` reports that JAGS headers or libraries are missing, install [JAGS 4.x](https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/JAGS/4.x/) and rerun the `mcp` installation. JAGS 5 is supported when `rjags` 5 is released.

# At a glance

`mcp` takes a list of formulas - one for each segment:

``` r
library(mcp)

model = list(
  response ~ 1,  # plateau (Intercept_1)
  ~ 0 + time,    # joined slope (time_2) at cp_1
  ~ 1 + time     # disjoined slope (Intercept_3, time_3) at cp_2
)

data = mcp_example_data("demo")
fit = mcp(model, data)
```

The change points are the values of the change-point variable (here `time`) where the model switches from one formula to the next. The first formula is just `response ~ predictors` and the most common formula for segment 2+ would be `~ predictors` (more details [here](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/formulas.html)).

You can do change point regression for a large number of models in a syntax that aligns with `lm()`/`glm()`/`brms`. E.g.:

`r sprintf("![](%s)", showcase_url)`

# Brief worked example

The following model infers the two change points between three segments. You can run this complete worked example (which fits the model and plots by default) in one line:

```{r demo-fit-mcp_example, results='hide', message=FALSE, fig.keep='none'}
library(mcp)
demo_fit = mcp_example("demo")  # Also check out other examples
```

See `demo_fit$example_code` for how it was generated, and explore more demos in `mcp_example()`. But for now, let's walk through the example manually:

```{r demo-fit-manual, results='hide', message=FALSE}
# Define the model
model = list(
  response ~ 1,  # plateau (Intercept_1)
  ~ 0 + time,    # joined slope (time_2) at cp_1.
  ~ 1 + time     # disjoined slope (Intercept_3, time_3) at cp_2
)

# Get example data and fit it: mcp(model, data, ...)
fit = mcp(model, demo_fit$data, sample = "both")
```

## Plot and summary

The default plot includes data, fitted lines drawn randomly from the posterior, and change point(s) posterior density for each chain. Here we also add the 95% central interval of the fitted values (`interval = "fitted"`):

```{r demo-plot}
plot(fit, interval = "fitted") + ggtitle("Regression with two change points")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# For mcp() documentation
ggplot2::ggsave("man/figures/mcp_demo.png", ggplot2::last_plot(), width = 6.00, height = 3.75, dpi = 125)
```

Use `summary()` to summarise the posterior distribution as well as sampling diagnostics:

```{r demo-summary}
summary(fit)
```

- `rhat` is the rank-normalized split-Rhat convergence diagnostic.
- `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail` are the effective sample sizes for the bulk and tails of the posterior. Warning thresholds can be changed with `mcp(..., diagnostics = list(rhat = 1.01, ess_bulk = 400, ess_tail = 400))`; `summary()` inherits these settings.
- In this case, we simulated data using `mcp` (see how in `demo_fit$example_code`) so the columns `sim` and `match` show true value and whether it was recovered.

`plot_pars(fit)` can be used to inspect the posteriors and convergence of all parameters. See the documentation of `plot_pars()` for many other plotting options. Here, we plot just the (population-level) change points. They often have "strange" posterior distributions, highlighting the need for a computational approach:

```{r demo-plot_pars}
plot_pars(fit, regex_pars = "cp_") + ggtitle("Change point posteriors")
```

Do a posterior predictive check to see if the model recovers the empirical distribution in the data:

```{r demo-pp_check}
pp_check(fit) + ggtitle("Posterior Predictive check for change point regression")
```

You can expect most generics from R, `posterior`, `tidybayes` to work on mcpfits. E.g., use `fitted(fit)` and `predict(fit)` to get fits and predictions for in-sample and out-of-sample data, use `as_draws(fit)` to get draws (see `?as_draws.mcpfit` for all formats), etc.

## Tests and model comparison

We can test (joint) probabilities in the model using `hypothesis()` ([see more here](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/comparison.html)). For example, what is the evidence (given priors) that the first change point (`cp_1`) is later than 30 against it being earlier than 30?

```{r demo-hypothesis}
hypothesis(fit, "cp_1 > 30")
```

For model comparisons, we can fit a null model and compare the predictive performance of the two models using (approximate) leave-one-out cross-validation ([see more here](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/comparison.html)). Let’s specify a null model where the first two segments are reduced to one straight line, i.e., removing the change point:

```{r demo-fit-null, results='hide', message=FALSE}
# Define the model
model_null = list(response ~ 1 + time)  # Intercept_1 and time_1

# Fit it
fit_null = mcp(model_null, demo_fit$data)
```

Leveraging the power of `loo::loo()`, we see that the two-change-points model is preferred (it is on top), and both `p_worse` and the `elpd_diff / se_diff` ratio indicate this preference is strong:

```{r demo-loo_compare}
fit_loo = loo(fit)
fit_null_loo = loo(fit_null)

loo::loo_compare(fit_loo, fit_null_loo)
```

# Learn more

The articles on the [mcp website](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/) go in-depth with the functionality of `mcp`:

**Modeling**

- [Understanding mcp formulas](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/formulas.html): how segments connect (joined `~ 0 + x` vs. disjoined `~ 1 + x`), parameter names, `same()`, and the model math.
- [Group-level (random) effects](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/group_effects.html): group-level intercepts, slopes, and change points, e.g., `(1 | id)` and `cp((1 | id))`.
- [Variance and other distributional parameters](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/dpar.html): change points in, e.g., the residual SD using `sigma(1 + x)`.
- [Time series and autocorrelation](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/arma.html): `ar()` and `ma()` terms, including change points in autocorrelation.

**Families**

- [Supported families and link functions](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/families.html): `gaussian()`, `binomial()`, `bernoulli()`, `poisson()`, and `negbinomial()`.
- [Poisson and negative binomial](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/poisson.html) and [Binomial and Bernoulli](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/binomial.html): worked examples, including rates via `offset()`.

**Inference**

- [Using priors](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/priors.html) and [Default priors](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/default_priors.html): set and check priors, including on change points.
- [Hypotheses and model comparison](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/comparison.html): `loo()`, directional `hypothesis()` tests, and Savage-Dickey Bayes factors.
- [Fits and predictions](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/predict.html): `fitted()` and `predict()`, including forecasting with future change points.
- [Plotting](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/plotting.html): `plot()`, `plot_dpar()`, `plot_pars()`, `pp_check()`, and your own `ggplot2` plots.
- [Missing responses and imputation](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/missing.html): change points in gaps of the data and imputations of missing responses.

**Implementation**

- [From formulas to sampler code](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/implementation.html): how `mcp` writes the JAGS model in `fit$jags_code`.
- [Diagnosing and fixing problems](https://lindeloev.github.io/mcp/articles/tips.html): convergence, speed, and common errors.
